How the practice works

Practice gives an English word and asks for the Latin. This page says how it chooses its cards and when a word comes back, on what evidence, and which numbers are simply our choice, as How we decide does for the words. Any of it can change: tell us where you think it wrong.

A roundWhen a word comes backThe evidenceOur own choicesWhat it does not doSources

A round

A round is 12 cards. A card shows the English headword and what narrows it down: its other English names, the gloss of the Latin word, the English of an example. You say the Latin aloud, turn the card, and mark yourself: Teneō (Got it) or Iterum (Again). Your progress stays on your device.

While the deck has new words, at most half of a round is repetition: first the words you missed, then those that have waited longest. The rest are new, and the two are mixed. With no new words left a round is all repetition; with nothing due, all new.

When a word comes back

  • A word you miss is due again in 10 minutes: in a later round, not in the same one.
  • Got right then, it is due the next day; then, each time you get it right, in 3–4 days, 6–8, 14–18 and 30–40, and after that every 30–40 days.
  • A new word you know at first sight is not shown again for 3–4 days.
  • A word missed at any stage starts again.
  • Days are calendar days, starting at 04:00 on your device. From 3 days up the wait is drawn at random within its range, so that words learned together do not all return together.
  • These are the shortest waits: when more words are due than a round has room for, the rest wait.

Until 15 November 2026 a word climbed through 10 minutes, 1 hour, then 1, 3, 7, 16 and 35 days, and a round took every due word before any new one. A reader who practised daily met a missed word four times in two days and, after a long session, a day of nothing but yesterday’s words.

The evidence

Testing yourself beats reading again. Undergraduates remembered 56% of a short prose passage a week later after being tested on it, and 42% after reading it again instead (Roediger & Karpicke 2006). Students who went on being tested on Swahili–English pairs they had already got right recalled about 80% a week later; those who were not, 33–36% (Karpicke & Roediger 2008). Over 61 studies the advantage averages half a standard deviation, and more where the answer is then shown (Rowland 2014).

Spaced beats massed. In experiments on verbal recall, most of them with young adults, repetitions spread over time gave 47% recall and repetitions run together 37%; spacing did better in 259 of 271 comparisons (Cepeda et al. 2006).

The best gap depends on how long you want to remember. For 1,354 adults who reviewed trivia facts once, it was about 20–40% of the delay when the test was a week away and 5–10% when it was a year away; too short a gap cost more than too long a one (Cepeda et al. 2008).

The exact schedule matters much less. Gaps that grow, often thought best since Landauer & Bjork (1978) taught names that way, show no reliable advantage in the end over equal gaps: 62% against 59% over 22 comparisons (Cepeda et al. 2006), and 49% against 46% for Japanese–English pairs practised over four weeks by 37 adults and tested eight weeks later, though the growing gaps kept more of the words recallable meanwhile (Kang et al. 2014). What did help, with vocabulary pairs learned in one sitting, was a first test after a delay and not at once (Karpicke & Roediger 2007), and a recall that took effort and succeeded (Pyc & Rawson 2009).

Our own choices

So the evidence supports the kind of thing the practice does, and settles none of its numbers.

  • The card. A cue, an answer to produce, then the answer shown: what the evidence supports best. That you mark yourself is our choice.
  • Ten minutes for a missed word. The evidence supports a real gap before the next attempt, not this number, which is Anki’s default for a forgotten card: 10 minutes, then a day (Anki Manual).
  • Waits that grow. Not shown to keep words better than equal ones, but they cost fewer repetitions, which a deck of thousands needs. Ours resemble those of SuperMemo’s SM-2: 1 day, 6 days, then each wait multiplied by a factor that starts at 2.5 (Woźniak 1990). No study settles 3 days against 4.
  • Stopping at 30–40 days. Our choice, and for words meant to last years probably too short: four people learning French or German words kept them better over years with sessions 56 days apart than with sessions 14 days apart (Bahrick et al. 1993), and SM-2 and Anki let the wait go on growing.
  • Three or four days for a word known at first sight. The rule with the least support. Four days is Anki’s default for a new card marked Easy; marked Good, it returns in 10 minutes and then the next day. We have one mark for both, and for a word you have only just looked up, one correct recall is weak proof (Karpicke & Roediger 2008).
  • Starting again after a miss, the random spread, the day that starts at 04:00. Anki’s practice. None is a finding.
  • Half of a round new, and mixed in. Our choice, for the reader’s interest; we found no study of it that we could read. The evidence leans the other way: repetition is what keeps a word (Karpicke & Roediger 2008), and Anki by default allows 20 new cards a day and 200 repetitions. So do the sums: a round brings at least 6 new words and has room for at most 6 repetitions, and a word needs three to five repetitions in its first month. A reader who takes new words every day soon has more words due than the rounds can hold, and the waits grow longer than those above. The rule gives up remembering for variety.

What it does not do

It keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. It does not adapt to you: every reader and every word gets the same waits, where a scheduler such as FSRS fits a model of memory to a person’s history and aims each card at a chosen chance of recall, 90% by default in Anki (Open Spaced Repetition; Anki Manual). It has two marks where Anki has four. A word got right long after it was due moves up one step, as if on time. It sets no limit on new words in a day. And it does not check your answer: you do.
